source_user: Advanced cluster case RDMA-5: Explain how RDMA changes the data path for multi-node GPU training or inference. Variant 5 must state assumptions, define a falsifiable hypothesis, name metrics, and include one failure or rollback condition.
source_assistant: An expert answer should distinguish model-domain mechanisms from runtime measurements. Required technical anchors: separate verbs, queues, memory registration, transport selection, bandwidth, latency, and fallback behavior; compare measured device counters with application-level communication time. It must report topology, workload, units, baselines, confounders, and evidence needed before claiming improvement.
corrected_answer:
Assume a multi-node GPU training or inference job whose nodes are connected by an RDMA-capable fabric; do not assume a particular NIC, switch, provider, RoCE configuration, or collective library. Explain the data path as a hypothesis, not as a guaranteed speedup: the application/collective library posts verbs work requests to send/receive or RDMA-read/write queues; the NIC uses registered memory and the selected transport to move bytes, while completion handling and any fallback path determine what the application observes. Distinguish the transport's mechanism from a measurement: RDMA can reduce host copies and CPU involvement and may lower communication latency, but queueing, registration, topology, congestion, PCIe/NIC placement, message size, synchronization, and fallback can dominate.

State the falsifiable hypothesis with units and scope, for example: under the same model, global batch, message sizes, node count, topology, software settings, and load, enabling the specified RDMA path reduces median and p99 all-reduce/all-gather communication time in milliseconds and improves effective GPU throughput in samples/s, without increasing error or tail latency beyond a predeclared limit, compared with a TCP or other controlled baseline. Record the exact topology (GPU-NIC affinity, links, bandwidth in Gb/s, hop count), workload and collective/message-size distribution, concurrency, warm-up, sample count, and confidence intervals.

Measure at both layers: application/collective start-to-completion time, per-operation latency in microseconds or milliseconds, achieved payload bandwidth in GB/s, overlap/step time, GPU utilization, CPU utilization, and timeout/error/fallback counts; also collect NIC/device counters for bytes, packets, retransmissions or RoCE congestion signals, queue depth/completions, registration/cache behavior, and link errors. Correlate timestamps so device counters are not mistaken for end-to-end benefit, and compare equal payloads and repetitions against the baseline. Check whether the negotiated transport is actually RDMA and whether the workload is using the intended queues; report missing counters rather than inventing them.

Define failure and rollback conditions before the test: any data-integrity error, repeated completion/transport errors, link or port instability, unexplained fallback, timeout, or a predeclared regression in p99 communication or end-to-end step time triggers rollback to the known-good path and preserves logs/configuration for diagnosis. Roll back gradually or disable the RDMA path only after draining work safely; do not claim causality from one run. Evidence required is a topology/configuration capture, baseline and treatment repetitions with controlled confounders, NIC and application counter correlation, failure-injection or link-failure behavior, and results across representative message sizes and load.

Security and safety limits: treat telemetry and configuration as potentially sensitive, do not expose credentials, and avoid changing transport settings in production without an approved canary, health checks, and an operational rollback.

State the falsifiable hypothesis with units and scope, for example: under the same model, global batch, message sizes, node count, topology, software settings, and load, enabling the specified RDMA path reduces median and p99 all-reduce/all-gather communication time in milliseconds and improves effective GPU throughput in samples/s, without increasing error or tail latency beyond a predeclared limit, compared with a TCP or other controlled baseline. Record the exact topology (GPU-NIC affinity, links, bandwidth in Gb/s, hop count), workload and collective/message-size distribution, concurrency, warm-up, sample count, and confidence intervals.

Measure at both layers: application/collective start-to-completion time, per-operation latency in microseconds or milliseconds, achieved payload bandwidth in GB/s, overlap/step time, GPU utilization, CPU utilization, and timeout/error/fallback counts; also collect NIC/device counters for bytes, packets, retransmissions or RoCE congestion signals, queue depth/completions, registration/cache behavior, and link errors. Correlate timestamps so device counters are not mistaken for end-to-end benefit, and compare equal payloads and repetitions against the baseline. Check whether the negotiated transport is actually RDMA and whether the workload is using the intended queues; report missing counters rather than inventing them.

Define failure and rollback conditions before the test: any data-integrity error, repeated completion/transport errors, link or port instability, unexplained fallback, timeout, or a predeclared regression in p99 communication or end-to-end step time triggers rollback to the known-good path and preserves logs/configuration for diagnosis. Roll back gradually or disable the RDMA path only after draining work safely; do not claim causality from one run. Evidence required is a topology/configuration capture, baseline and treatment repetitions with controlled confounders, NIC and application counter correlation, failure-injection or link-failure behavior, and results across representative message sizes and load.

Security and safety limits: treat telemetry and configuration as potentially sensitive, do not expose credentials, and avoid changing transport settings in production without an approved canary, health checks, and an operational rollback.
